paragraphs.heading: A cloud in space
paragraphs.text: Nebula is Latin for cloud or fog. A nebula is a distinct glowing part of the interstellar medium, made of hydrogen, which may be ionized, neutral or molecular, along with cosmic dust. Many nebulae are places where stars form; one example is the Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula. The material left over after stars form is thought to make planets and other objects of a planetary system.

paragraphs.heading: Huge but almost empty
paragraphs.text: Most nebulae are enormous, and some are hundreds of light-years across. Yet they are extremely thin: Earth's air has about 10¹⁹ molecules per cubic centimetre, while the densest nebulae can have about 10⁴. A nebula you can see from Earth with your eyes would look bigger from close by, but not brighter. The Orion Nebula, the brightest in the sky, covers twice the angular diameter of the full Moon and can be seen with the naked eye, yet early astronomers missed it.

paragraphs.heading: Why they shine
paragraphs.text: Many nebulae glow through fluorescence caused by hot stars inside them. Others are so diffuse that they can only be picked up with long exposures and special filters. Some are lit in a changing way by T Tauri variable stars. Others shine by reflected starlight: in 1912 Vesto Slipher showed that the nebula around the star Merope has the same spectrum as the Pleiades open cluster.

paragraphs.heading: Early sightings
paragraphs.text: Around 150 AD, Ptolemy's Almagest listed five stars that looked nebulous, and a patch of haze between Ursa Major and Leo that belonged to no star. In his Book of Fixed Stars (964), the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi mentioned the first true nebula, rather than a star cluster: a little cloud where the Andromeda Galaxy is. In 1610 Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc found the Orion Nebula with a telescope, and Christiaan Huygens made the first detailed study of it in 1659.

paragraphs.heading: The catalogues grow
paragraphs.text: Edmond Halley published a list of six nebulae in 1715, and the count rose steadily through that century. By 1781 Charles Messier had catalogued 103, now called Messier objects; he was looking for comets, and these were things that could be mistaken for them. William Herschel and his sister Caroline then added far more, in catalogues of a thousand in 1786, another thousand in 1789, and a final 510 in 1802.

paragraphs.heading: Gas, stars or galaxies
paragraphs.text: At first the word nebula covered any diffuse object in the sky, galaxies included, so the Andromeda Galaxy was once the Andromeda Nebula. From 1864 William Huggins studied the spectra of about 70 nebulae: roughly a third had the emission spectrum of a gas, and the rest showed a continuous spectrum and were thought to be masses of stars. In 1922 Edwin Hubble announced that nearly all nebulae are linked to stars and lit by starlight. In 1923, following the Great Debate, astronomers saw that many so-called nebulae were really galaxies far from the Milky Way.
